issues.description: The manuscript explicitly warns in both the abstract and methods/results sections that all reported statistics, means, SDs, and inferential test results are generated from a randomized/simulated Qualtrics dataset, not from actual data collection. Despite this disclaimer, the results section is written in the past tense as if data were collected and analysed, with specific statistics interpreted and discussed as if real. This fundamentally undermines the validity of every statistical claim in the manuscript. No real findings exist to evaluate.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.] ... A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.description: The procedures section states that 'Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions,' meaning participants self-selected into experimental conditions rather than being randomly assigned. This completely invalidates any causal inference about the effect of intervention or identifiability on donation or feelings. The original studies used strict random assignment to between-subjects conditions. Self-selection introduces severe confounding: participants who choose to learn about the identifiable victim effect likely differ systematically from those who do not.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The design section declares this is a 'within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables,' but the original studies used strictly between-subjects designs. A within-subject design for this paradigm is fundamentally incompatible with the intervention manipulation: once participants learn about the identifiable victim effect, that knowledge cannot be removed for subsequent conditions. Moreover, seeing all victim types (identifiable, statistical, joint) within the same session introduces demand characteristics and contrast effects that would severely confound the identifiable victim effect being measured. The analysis then uses between-subjects F-tests and t-tests, contradicting the stated within-subject design.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.description: The replication uses an 'imaginary donation' (participants indicate a hypothetical dollar amount from $0–$5) rather than actual monetary donations. The original study gave participants $5 in real cash and measured actual giving behaviour. Real money paradigms and hypothetical donation paradigms are not psychologically equivalent; willingness-to-donate hypothetically is known to systematically overestimate real giving and may have different sensitivity to affective manipulations. This is a major construct validity deviation that is listed as 'Different' in Table 6 but its theoretical implications for the key dependent variable are not adequately discussed.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The results text reports 'participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).' However, computing marginal means from Table 7 yields approximately M=2.538 for the identifiable condition and M=2.246 for the statistical condition—precisely opposite to what the text claims. The labels appear to have been reversed in the text. Additionally, M=2.24 and SD=1.67 do not correspond to any cell in Table 7 for the identifiable victim condition.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: The abstract states 'we found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect,' yet Table 9 reports a significant two-way interaction effect of identifiability × intervention on donation, F(2, 994)=4.25, p=.015. A significant interaction effect is precisely evidence that the intervention (analytical reasoning manipulation) has a differential effect across victim types—i.e., it IS evidence about analytical reasoning's impact on the identifiable victim effect. The abstract's conclusion directly contradicts the reported inferential test.
issues.quote: we found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect... [Table 9] Interaction Replication | 2 | 4.25 | .015*

issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts 'An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims' (identifiable > statistical). However, the abstract concludes 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics'—the exact opposite direction. Furthermore, the actual post-hoc finding in Table 14 shows significance only between the statistical and joint conditions (not identifiable vs. statistical), with statistical victims rated higher in perceived impact than joint-condition victims. Neither the abstract nor the post-hoc results support Hypothesis 6 as stated.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics. [Hypothesis 6]: An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims.

issues.description: Table 9 uses residual df=994 for the 2×3 ANOVA (consistent with N=1000, 6 cells), but Table 11 reports the contrast t-test with df=998, implying a simple two-group t-test on the full N=1000 ignoring the design's 6-cell structure. These models are not equivalent and use different error terms. Within a single study's results section, the same underlying dataset should not shift between residual df=994 and df=998 without explanation of which model was used and why.
issues.quote: Replication | 2 | 3.58 | .028* [df=2, Residual=994] ... Replication: Identifiable/no intervention ... t(998)=0.59

issues.description: Table 1 reports the same F-statistic, df, and p-value for each individual group mean row within a factor. For example, both 'Identifiable victim' (M=2.12) and 'Statistical victim' (M=1.21) are given the same F(1,115)=6.75, p<.05, ηp²=.06. In ANOVA, the F-statistic belongs to the factor as a whole, not to individual group means. Individual group means do not have separate F-statistics. This formatting error fundamentally misrepresents ANOVA output and could mislead readers about the nature of the statistical test.

Table 10 reports the Identifiable vs. Statistical post-hoc comparison as t(994)=-2.40, d=0.076, 95% CI [-0.05, 0.20], pBonferroni=.049. The 95% CI for the effect size crosses zero (lower bound -0.05), which is inconsistent with a p-value that is statistically significant at α=.05. A CI that includes zero should correspond to a non-significant result. Similarly, Table 14 reports Statistical vs. Joint as d=0.08, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.23], pBonferroni=.041, where again the CI crosses zero. These are contradictory and indicate errors in either the p-value or CI calculation.

The simulated sample has a mean age of 67.80 years (SD=30.10) and an age range of 18–120 years. A mean age of 67.80 is implausible for an MTurk sample, which typically skews toward 25–45 years old. An age range reaching 120 years is biologically impossible for current respondents. These values are clearly artifacts of random data generation (Qualtrics uniform distribution across a wide numeric range) rather than plausible participant characteristics. This underscores the problem of using fake data to simulate results.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males)... Age range (years) | Not specified | 18-120 | 18-120

issues.description: The replication applies the explicit intervention (teaching about the identifiable victim effect) to the joint condition, a combination that did not exist in either Study 1 or Study 3 of the original. This creates a new experimental cell not derived from either original study and introduces an untested combination of manipulations. The joint condition in Study 3 was designed as an implicit manipulation; adding explicit intervention to it conflates two theoretically distinct debiasing mechanisms. This is listed as a deviation but its theoretical implications for comparing implicit vs. explicit effects are not adequately analyzed.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.description: Throughout the results and discussion, causal language is used to describe the effects (e.g., 'participants who faced a statistical victim... tended to donate more,' 'thinking analytically about your helping behaviour would reduce your motivation'). Given that participants self-selected their conditions rather than being randomly assigned, any differences between conditions are systematically confounded by participant characteristics that drove condition choice. Causal inference requires random assignment, which is absent here.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)... thinking analytically about your helping behaviour would reduce your motivation to offer assistance to a single beneficiary.

issues.description: The paper attributes the affect-driven component of the identifiable victim effect to the 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973). The availability heuristic concerns ease of mentally retrieving instances and is a frequency/probability judgment heuristic. The mechanism by which identifiable victims elicit more giving is better characterized by the 'affect heuristic' (prominently discussed in Slovic et al., 2007, which is even cited in the references) or affect/imagery mechanisms. Small et al. (2007) themselves frame this as an affective, not availability-based, process. This is a theoretical mischaracterization of the core mechanism under study.
issues.quote: The 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual (Small & Loewenstein, 2003). The information we receive about this person may elicit stronger affective reactions such as sympathy and distress.

issues.description: The original study used ordered probit regression as the primary analysis for the donation outcome (a 6-point ordinal scale: $0–$5), recognizing the ordinal nature of the DV. The replication excludes this analysis entirely, replacing it with ANOVA, which assumes a continuous, normally distributed DV. This is noted in Table 5 ('This test would not be conducted in the replication') but no statistical or methodological justification is provided. Excluding the original study's primary analytic approach affects comparability and could systematically inflate or deflate effect size estimates on ordinal data.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The Methods section does not describe the experimental procedure in the manuscript itself, instead redirecting readers entirely to an external Qualtrics survey link and a supplementary Google Doc. Essential procedural details necessary for evaluating and replicating the study—including exact survey instructions, question wording, randomization procedure, condition assignment mechanism, timing, and attention check content—are absent from the peer-reviewed manuscript. External links may become unavailable and cannot be considered part of the permanent scientific record.
issues.quote: The session of 'Procedure' in the supplementary summarizes the procedure of the current replication study. For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below.

issues.description: The segregated feeling items (upsetting, sympathy, touched, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, perceived impact) are listed in Table 5 but their operationalization is not described anywhere in the manuscript. The scale format, response anchors, number of items per construct, exact question wording, and the method for aggregating them into the composite 'aggregated feelings' measure are all absent. This makes the measures impossible to evaluate for construct validity or to replicate.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.description: The manuscript states that 'participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check,' yet the number of participants excluded under each criterion is never reported. The final analysis N=1000 appears to be the initial generated sample, not a post-exclusion count. Pre-registration and replication standards require transparent reporting of how many participants were excluded and for which reasons to evaluate whether exclusions could have influenced results.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts that 'identifiable victims elicit higher perceived impact than statistical victims.' The only statistically significant post-hoc finding for perceived impact (Table 14) is between the statistical victim condition and the joint condition (p=.041), with statistical victims rated higher than joint-condition victims. This comparison (Statistical vs. Joint) does not test Hypothesis 6 at all. The comparison directly specified by Hypothesis 6 (Identifiable vs. Statistical) is not significant (p=1.000 Bonferroni-corrected). The manuscript nevertheless frames the extension results as supporting the hypothesis.
issues.quote: Significant differences were found between the statistical victim condition and the joint condition, t(994)=2.47, SE=0.11, p=.041... [Hypothesis 6]: An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims.

issues.description: The manuscript claims to be a pre-registered study ('Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period') and states data collection was completed before analyses, yet the [IMPORTANT] notes reveal results were generated from simulated random data and 'will be updated following data collection.' This creates fundamental ambiguity about whether the pre-registration was filed before or after actual data collection, and whether the analysis code and decisions described were genuinely prospective. The pre-registration link is provided but the review link is restricted, making verification impossible.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period... [IMPORTANT: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection.]

issues.description: The original study recruited participants from a university student center (young, educated, US-based), while this replication uses Amazon Mechanical Turk workers. MTurk samples differ on dimensions directly relevant to charitable giving: they are more financially constrained, more experienced with online tasks (reducing ecological validity of donation scenarios), more diverse in age, and may have differing baseline rates of charitable behavior. The replication classifies this as a 'different' contextual variable but does not discuss how this population shift could moderate the identifiable victim effect being tested.
issues.quote: Physical settings: Different | Online survey: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania.

issues.description: Table 6 classifies the replication as 'close to very close replication' using the Lebel et al. (2018) framework, yet Table 6 itself lists three design facets as 'Different' (DV stimuli, physical settings, contextual variables) and two as 'Similar' (DV operationalization, IV stimuli). Under Lebel et al.'s framework, 'Different' physical settings alone places the study at 'very close replication' at best; multiple 'Different' facets and a fundamentally altered DV (hypothetical vs. real donation) arguably place it in the 'close replication' category or lower.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication | [Table shows DV stimuli: Different, Physical settings: Different, Contextual variables: Different]

issues.description: The manuscript contains a table numbering error: the classification table in the Replication Evaluation section is labeled 'Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a close to very close replication' in the text, yet this table is labeled Table 6 in the actual table header. This also means the table labeled Table 7 in the Results section (descriptive statistics) is referenced by the same number as the earlier table in Methods. This creates confusion when cross-referencing tables and suggests insufficient manuscript proofreading.
issues.quote: Figure 2 specifies the classification of the replications... Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a 'close to very close replication'... [But the actual table header reads] Table 6: Classification of the replication.

issues.description: The name 'Slovic' is consistently misspelled as 'Solvic' in the Introduction ('Solvic, 2007' and 'Solvic, 2010'). More critically, 'Solvic (2010)' is cited in the introduction but does not appear in the reference list, constituting an uncited reference. Additionally, the 2007 citation is correctly spelled 'Slovic (2007)' in the reference list, meaning the same author appears with two different spellings in the same section.
issues.quote: Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks of the phenomenon... The study to be replicated was also covered in the meta-analysis conducted by Lee and Feeley (2016)... (Solvic, 2010).

issues.description: The original study gave participants real cash ($5) from a prior survey and measured actual allocation of those funds to charity. The replication explicitly removes this incentive structure ('No reward acquired from a pre-survey: Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation'). The real-money endowment creates loss aversion and psychological ownership that may be critical to activating the affective responses underlying the identifiable victim effect. Without real money, the task is purely hypothetical and may not engage the same motivational and affective processes.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey: Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation.

issues.description: The study combines five distinct affective/evaluative items (being upset, being touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness) into a single 'aggregated feelings' composite score that serves as a key dependent variable. No psychometric justification for this aggregation is provided—no Cronbach's alpha, factor analysis, or theoretical rationale explaining why these theoretically distinct constructs (affect vs. moral judgment vs. behavioral appropriateness) should be combined into one score is reported. The original study reported these items separately; creating an unvalidated composite adds analytic decisions not present in the original.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling... We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on the aggregated feelings.

issues.description: Multiple mandatory linked resources in the manuscript contain placeholder text rather than actual links (e.g., 'Cloud folder for presentation: <enter link here>', 'Cloud folder for peer reviews: <enter link here>'). The word count is presented in brackets as '[7394]' suggesting it is a template field. These indicate the manuscript was submitted in an incomplete state, preventing proper evaluation of the study materials, peer review records, and presentation materials that would normally inform replication quality assessment.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here> | Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here> | Word: abstract – [136], manuscript - [7394]
